article_text:
When Justin Lothrop first came across Ursula Wills’ short story “The Wicker Husband” online in 2021, the Votiv Films producer immediately knew that it was material worth championing. The offbeat fantasy fable, which at its core explores themes of jealousy and the transformative power of love, was just the kind of unique IP that the Seattle and L.A.-based banner looks to back.

“It hadn’t been published anywhere,” Lothrop recalls of Wills’ story, which is the source material for Olivia Colman starrer Wicker that releases in the U.S. tomorrow (October 23) via Black Bear. “She was just writing them and putting them up on a website somewhere.”

Related Stories

‘Wicker’ Review: Olivia Colman And Peter Dinklage Turn Alexander Skarsgard Into A Sexy Basket Case In Comic Fable That’s Pure Delight

For Votiv founder Brent Stiefel and Lothrop, who have built the company’s business around finding distinctive material and championing stories that might otherwise struggle to reach the screen – think Sydney Sweeney boxing title Christy and Rose Byrne comedy-drama Tow –, the premise was an immediate draw. Lothrop quickly optioned the story and sent it to producer Brad Zimmerman of Yoki, Inc., the production company founded with filmmaker David Michôd.

Watch on Deadline

Votiv and Yoki would ultimately enlist Save Yourselves! filmmakers Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson to write and direct the project that would later attach Colman and her South Of The River Pictures banner to embrace a film that is anything but conventional.

Wicker is an audacious comedic fable about sex, marriage and the absurdities of social convention. It tells the wholly original love story of an ostracized fisherwoman, played by Colman, who commissions a husband to be made by the local basketmaker, played by Peter Dinklage. When her wicker husband (Alexander Skarsgård) proves more spectacular than she ever imagined, his soulful spirit and unique prowess awaken something inside of her, setting off a wave of jealousy, fascination and upheaval that threatens the very fabric of village life. Elizabeth Debicki, Marli Sui and Nabhaan Rizwan also star.

Topic Studios and Tango financed the title. Producers are Ed Sinclair, Tom Carver, Lothrop, Zimmerman, Lia Buman, Ryan Heller, Colman, Brent Stiefel, Michôd, Tim Headington, Michael Bloom, Andrea Cornwell and Oliver Kassman.

When Colman was sent the project at script stage to potentially play the main character, the material immediately stood out to her.

“I’m always excited if there’s something I haven’t read before,” she says. “It’s amazing how many similar scripts turn up and this was just a total godsend, a bolt out of the blue. I’ve never seen anything like it before.”

Creative fit

After optioning Wills’ story, Lothrop and Zimmerman were keen to attach husband and wife writing-directing duo Wilson and Fischer, the filmmakers behind 2020 Sundance sci-fi comedy Save Yourselves! , because they felt “they would really get the material.”

“I always loved the way they approached theme,” says Lothrop. “ Save Yourselves! was such a unique movie that had a lot to say about the world and an allegory for climate change and how we are approaching that. So, their ability to bring out themes through these visually unique spaces was interesting in terms of how their brains work.”

He admits that Wills’ short story didn’t have as many patriarchal themes as the feature film does, with the original work focusing more on “jealousy” and “people’s reactions to love that they don’t understand” but Wilson and Fischer really leaned in on the construct of marriage and how to defy gender expectations in the script.

“They are really able to unpick the little intricate complexities of a relationship,” says Zimmerman. “They brought a lot more to the patriarchal approach that they took and to be able to balance that complexity with a more fantastical approach is a really delicate tonal balance. It’s a unique gift to bring the warmth and the humor but not shy away from the more difficult parts of talking about relationships and the challenges that we have as human beings.”

Fischer and Wilson completed the script in two weeks in 2021 while in quarantine, before producers sent it to Colman. The Wicked Little Letters and The Roses actor says she immediately felt drawn to this character whose independence is strengthened, rather than compromised, by love.

“She was on her own, but she had so much power and she was perfectly happy with herself,” Colman says. “Finding the right partner didn’t halve her power, but it enhanced it. There’s something beautiful about the two of them and the bomb that gets set off in the village when they realize that they’ve been doing it wrong. And it’s a lovely look at women and their position and what love should look like.”

She continues: “I think imbalance always interests me and I never want to not mention it. But this is done with such humour and such a light touch and it’s not beating anyone over the head with it, but rather saying that this is probably how it used to be and this is how we don’t want it to be. The central love is of total equality and that is important to me.”

At this point, Colman and her South Of The River Pictures banner, which she founded in 2019 with her husband and screenwriter Ed Sinclair and MD Tom Carver, opted to board the project from a production standpoint as they felt they could add value to the project.

“One thing that was obvious from the start is that it had a very sort of British sensibility,” says Sinclair, the writer and creator of Sky/HBO drama series Landscapers . “Al and El are from American indie comedy and there’s a very thin line between that and British indie TV comedy. They had watched all the shows that we all grew up with, many of which Olivia had been in, so we immediately had a sense that we could be really useful in that respect.”

Sinclair continues: “As a writer, I tend to write stuff that tonally sits at a very specific place that’s comic and dark and Wicker has that brilliantly. I know from experience how brilliant but also how hard it can be to deliver that on screen and the number of wrong turns you can take. So, it felt like we could be a really useful support for them on that front. And, as a company, we want to back brilliant, creative people who are willing to take a risk. There’s something totally thrilling about that because we don’t really see it as a risk, we see it as terrific fun.”

Indeed, having a main love interest made out of wicker is a risky proposition in the current marketplace but Carver says that the originality of the script and tone was always going to be “a blessing or a curse.”

“Fortunately, we found the right partners, and we found the right people who saw it as a blessing and that comes from the fantastic script and Olivia’s attachment,” he says.

Black Bear pre-sold the title at AFM in 2023 and the project shot in Hungary September-November 2024. While in post-production, the team decided to hold back for a Sundance bow, where it premiered earlier this year. Black Bear shortly took U.S. rights after its premiere and the company is also releasing the film in the UK on October 30.

Betting on “future comps”

For Votiv, Wicker is a clear example of the kinds of singular stories that it looks to source and bring to writers and directors. “The way we like to approach things, because we are such a small company, is by trying to do things that feel unique to the marketplace,” he says. “Broadly speaking, it allows us to find a little space for ourselves.

“There are plenty of companies that do great work that are a little more down the middle than what we do and so, as a result, unfortunately because a lot of these stories aren’t being told, what ends up starting to feel unique are stories like Christy and Tow and Wicker and these feel like stories that Hollywood has ignored. We’ve found that there are a lot of stories about strong women that aren’t being told and there’s an opportunity for us to be able to tell some of them. I think we’ve just been lucky to get a few of these off of the ground.”

Zimmerman adds: “A film like this was very hard to comp as we were putting it together. It’s very fantastical in tone and specific and is a bold statement. But I want to be making the movies that are the future comps, not the ones that are trying to mimic the past. We want to try and give audiences something new and it’s a really hard thing to do. No one can totally invent the wheel, but we have to try.”

"现代美术家，京都大学防灾研究所特定教授。以京都・NY为据点活动。1980年代入选中谷芙二子氏设立的录像画廊SCAN公开征集展，1986年在纽约现代美术馆（MoMA）由芭芭拉·伦敦策划的“NEW VIDEO JAPAN”中完成国际出道。1990年代起在武藏野美术大学与ATR从事教育与研究，1999年因情感语音对话研究在东京大学取得工学博士学位。2001年起在纽鲍豪斯的乔治·凯佩什创立的麻省理工学院 Center for Advanced Visual Studies（现 MIT Program in Art, Culture and Technology）进行研究，2002～04年担任艺术家研究员。2005年起在京都大学从事教育与研究。提倡将日本美重新理解为形式的“文化计算”，运用声音、振动、流体、重力等探究自然现象生成形态的条件。2016年度作为文化厅文化交流使在NY时报广场发表《Sound of Ikebana: Spring》。目前在京大防灾研究所研究自然与流体的艺术。作品被MoMA、富山县美术馆、建仁寺、岛津制作所等收藏。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artexhibition.jp/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/13-3.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "土佐尚子", "credit": "美術展ナビ", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在生成式AI急速进化、“人类描绘”“创造图像”的根本意义发生动摇的当下，土佐尚子约40年来持续以先锐科技凝视自然现象本身动态的轨迹，将给我们带来极为鲜明的视角。从被MoMA收藏的初期录像艺术，到令世界惊叹的互动作品，再到以最新声音振动将琳派生命感升华至现代绘画的首次公开新作，美与科技融合的压倒性空间体验不容错过。在京都历史悠久、充满光线的空间中，不妨细细感受自然与人类交织出的“生成之神秘”。（美术展Navi）", "translated": true}]

article_text:
京都市京セラ美術館（京都市左京区）で、「現代美術家 土佐尚子展「生成されるものたち」―アート&テクノロジーの現在地―」が11月7日から本館1階「光の広間」にて開催されます（入場無料）。本展は、土佐が約40年にわたり探究してきた「自然が像を生み出す条件」をたどりながら、生成AI時代における人間、自然、テクノロジー、芸術の関係にあらためて焦点が当てられます。

現代美術家 土佐尚子展「生成されるものたち」 ―アート&テクノロジーの現在地―

会場：京都市京セラ美術館 本館1階「光の広間」（京都市左京区岡崎円勝寺町124）

会期：2026年11月7日（土）～22日（日）

開館時間：10:00～18:00

休館日：月曜日

入場料：無料

アクセス： 地下鉄東西線「東山駅」より徒歩約8分 市バス「岡崎公園 美術館・平安神宮前」下車すぐ

詳細は、 展覧会公式HP まで。

生成AI時代に問い直す、「像は誰がつくるのか」

土佐尚子は、音・空気・重力・流体という自然そのものが描く像を、40年以上追究してきたアーティストです。彼女の作品における「生成」とは、AIに画像をつくらせることではありません。自然現象が形を生み出す条件をつくり、人間の眼では捉えられない一瞬を、テクノロジーによって可視化することです。その作家性や制作スタイルは、以下のとおりまとめることができます。

・作家自身が形を描くのではなく、音、空気、振動、重力、流体に形を生み出させる ・高速度カメラを、記録装置ではなく「筆に代わる制作装置」として用いる ・1985年の《An Expression》から現在まで、「見えない力が、どのように像になるのか」を問い続ける ・日本文化に内在する、余白、うつろい、非対称性、気韻生動を、装飾様式ではなく「生成の原理」として捉え直す ・アートとテクノロジーの融合そのものではなく、テクノロジーを通して自然と人間の関係を問い直す

本展では、土佐が約40年にわたり探究してきた「自然が像を生み出す条件」をたどりながら、生成AI時代における人間、自然、テクノロジー、芸術の関係を4つの時代・テーマに分けて構成・紹介されます。

展示構成

【第1章】 感覚変換・身体・意識の変容（1980年代作品）

初期の映像表現・ビデオアート作品を展開。表情や身体の微細な動きから言葉以前の情動を捉えた、MoMA収蔵作品《An Expression》（1985）や《ECSTASY》（1986）、《GUSH!》（1989）など、作家の原点となる作品が紹介されます。

【第2章】感情・対話・物語（1990年代～2000年代作品）

人工知能（AI）や音響解析技術を取り入れ、人間の声の抑揚や感情をリアルタイムで認識・対話するインタラクティブ・アートに挑戦した時期の作品群。赤ちゃんの姿をしたAIが感情豊かに反応する《Neuro-Baby》や、声から詩を紡ぎ出す《Interactive Poem》などが展示されます。

【第3章】 カルチュラル・コンピューティング（2010年代～2025年作品）

日本文化に息づく禅の精神や水墨画、いけばなの美学をコンピュータ・アルゴリズムへと「翻訳」・構造化した代表作群。MITで発表され話題となった《Zenetic Computer》、音の振動によって絵具が飛び跳ね一瞬の花の姿を見せる《Sound of Ikebana》、流体・重力・衝突が生む形態を可視化した《Genesis》、植物の枯れゆく時間を肉眼を超えた映像で表現した《うつろひ》などがダイナミックに展開されます。

【第4章】自然・気韻生動・テクノロジー（2026年～新作）

琳派の美意識を再解釈し、金地の上に流体や音振動が描き出す有機的な生命感を結びつけた新作《土佐琳派：気韻生動》シリーズ、および風と音の振動から生み出された屏風作品《風神》が初公開されます。筆を使わず、テクノロジーを媒介として「自然そのものに絵を描かせる」という新たな日本絵画の境地が提示されます。

関連イベント『対談プログラム「TALK+」』にも要注目

会期中、アート・デザイン・科学・伝統芸能の第一線で活躍する識者・有識者をゲストに迎え、多角的なテーマで対談イベントが開催されます。（会場：光の広間／参加無料）

アートを未来へつなぐ『アートエコシステム』としての「TALK+」～作品を「つくる」だけでなく、「価値を育て、未来へ残す」～

作品の価値は、アーティストが制作しただけでは社会に定着しません。作品を歴史の中に位置づける人、批評する人、研究する人、発表・販売する人、収蔵・保存する人、社会へ伝える人、そして実際に体験する人がつながることで、作品は一時的な発表を超え、次の世代に継承される文化資産になります。本展が提案する「アートエコシステム」とは、次の役割を循環させる仕組みです。

・アーティストが作品を創造する ・美術史家や批評家が、作品を歴史と社会の中に位置づける ・美術館と学芸員が、作品を研究し、展示し、収蔵・保存する ・ギャラリーとコレクターが、作品の価値を市場の中で育てる ・科学者と研究者が、技術や鑑賞体験を検証する ・企業が、共同研究や技術協力を通して社会実装につなげる ・メディアが、作品の意味を社会へ伝える ・観客が、作品を体験し、新たな解釈を生み出す

「TALK＋」は、これらの異なる役割を担う人々を一つの展覧会に集め、創造、批評、研究、発信、流通、収蔵、継承の循環を可視化する試みです。単なるトークイベントではなく、日本のメディアアートを、未来へ残すべき文化資産として考えるための実践の場です。

会期中に予定されているプログラム一覧

■11月7日（土）1部10:00～11:30｜2部16:00～18:30 オープニング1部「コレクションは未来を編集する」 長谷川祐子Yuko Hasegawa（キュレーター）によるビデオメッセージ 大林剛郎（大林組会長・アートコレクター）×土佐尚子

オープニング2部「日本美術は、翻訳できるのか」 太田梨紗子（美術史家）と土佐尚子による展示作品説明 高橋信也（本展キュラトリアルアドバイザー・京都市参事）×土佐尚子

■11月8日（日） 14:00～16:00 「見抜く、位置づける、残す」 アートの価値・まだ評価されていない作品の何を見るのか 山本豊津（東京画廊）×土佐尚子

■11月14日（土）14:00～16:00 「アートは未来を発明できるか」 伊東順二氏（美術評論家）×土佐尚子

■11月15日（日）14:00～16:00「自然は絵を描けるか」 長谷川等伯・琳派から、土佐尚子の「生成する日本絵画」へFrank Feltens（シアトル美術館チーフキュレーター）×土佐尚子＊同時通訳付き

■11月21日（土）1部13:30～15:00｜2部15:30～17:00 1部「作者は、どこにいるのか」 石津智大氏（関西大学教授・神経美学）×土佐尚子 2部「文化は受け継ぐ、アートは揺さぶる」 山本浩貴氏（実践女子大学）×土佐尚子

■11月22日（日）14:00～16:00 「いのちの一瞬を、どう生けるか」 池坊いけばなと《Sound of Ikebana》－－花・時間・自然のかたち 池坊専好（池坊次期家元）×土佐尚子

「TALK+」は事前申込制です。定員の都合上、先着順となるため席を用意できない可能性があります。申込みはお早めに。

現代美術家 土佐尚子 プロフィール

現代美術家、京都大学防災研究所特定教授。京都・NYを拠点に活動。1980年代に中谷芙二子氏が設立したビデオギャラリーSCANの公募展に入選し、1986年ニューヨーク近代美術館（MoMA）のバーバラ・ロンドン企画「NEW VIDEO JAPAN」で国際デビュー。1990年代より武蔵野美術大学とATRで教育研究に携わり、1999年、東京大学で感情音声対話の研究により工学博士号を取得。2001年よりニューバウハウスのジョージ・ケペシュが創立したマサチューセッツ工科大学 Center for Advanced Visual Studies（現 MIT Program in Art, Culture and Technology）で研究し、2002～04年アーティスト・フェローを務めた。2005年より京都大学で教育研究に従事。日本美を型として捉え直す「カルチュラル・コンピューティング」を提唱し、音、振動、流体、重力などを用いて自然現象が形を生む条件を探究する。2016年度には文化庁文化交流使としてNYタイムズスクエアで《Sound of Ikebana: Spring》を発表。現在、京大防災研究所で自然と流体のアートを研究している。作品はMoMA、富山県美術館、建仁寺、島津製作所等に収蔵。

生成AIの急速な進化によって「人間が描くこと」「像をつくること」の根源的な意味が揺らぐ現代において、約40年間にわたり自然現象そのもののダイナミズムを先鋭的なテクノロジーで見つめ続けてきた土佐尚子の軌跡は、私たちに極めて鮮烈な視座をもたらしてくれます。MoMAに収蔵された初期ビデオアートから、世界を驚かせたインタラクティブ作品、そして琳派の生命感を最新の音振動によって現代絵画へと昇華させた初公開の新作まで、美とテクノロジーが融合した圧倒的な空間体験は必見です。京都の歴史ある光あふれる空間で、自然と人間が織りなす「生成の神秘」にじっくりと触れてみてはいかがでしょうか。（美術展ナビ）

article_text:
Carole Bellaïche: What the image is still searching for

With À ta recherche ( In Search of You ), Carole Bellaïche continues an artistic practice that never merely photographs reality, but questions what lingers within it. For her, the image is not a way of stopping time, but an unstable surface where the present, memory and absence overlap. To photograph is less about preserving than about placing what remains in tension with what has disappeared. The title of the book immediately introduces this ambiguity. À ta recherche implies a research, but also an impossibility: that of ever fully finding what one is looking for. Photography thus becomes the very space of this quest, with all the displacement, projection and gaps it entails. This approach finds a particularly fertile counterpoint in Yannick Haenel’s text. Literature does not explain the images, any more than the photographs illustrate the text: together, they construct a mental territory in which the visible is constantly traversed by what escapes it.

In À ta recherche , Carole Bellaïche thus shifts documentary photography towards a more elusive territory, where the image becomes both an experience of memory and an instrument of thought. What matters is no longer simply what the photograph shows, but what it brings back afterwards: a sensation, an absence, an incomplete story, sometimes even an image we thought we had forgotten. It is in this space between – between appearance and disappearance, presence and absence, reality and memory -that the strength of her work lies today.

Instagram : @carolebellaiche Website : www.carolebellaiche.com

“A ta recherche” by Carole Bellaiche and Yannick Haenel, édition Gallimard

The beginning of a series sometimes comes from a particular encounter. What was the starting point for À ta recherche ?

Carole Bellaïche: I started this series five years ago, photographing this young couple, with whom I immediately felt a real connection, in the Bois de Vincennes. They were both very comfortable in front of the camera, so I had fun creating very theatrical double-exposure images, inspired by the book Spoon River by the Italian master Mario Giacomelli. I very quickly discovered in the young woman a naturalness that I had hardly ever photographed before, and it made me want to continue this adventure.

To photograph intimacy: is it about crossing a boundary or abolishing a distance?

Carole Bellaïche: It is undoubtedly about crossing a barrier. It means getting closer, looking, provoking something in my subjects. There is something voyeuristic and provocative about it as well. I also try to convey messages through my images. Images of love are beautiful, poetic images that make you dream, and that is what I want to translate. And despite the few staged elements, the intimacy is real because they are a real couple.

You say that you want to translate love into images. What can photography capture that words cannot hold on to?

Carole Bellaïche: Everything! My language is really photography. That is how I have always expressed myself. The immediacy of an image triggers emotions and sensations that are much easier to capture than with words. Obviously, for me, it is easier to make images than to write. With actresses, for example, my relationship with them is photographic. It is my language.

The book then brings literature into your photographic language. How did your encounter with Yannick Haenel come about?

Carole Bellaïche: As I said earlier, I made the images for this book inspired by Giacomelli, and I was advised to meet Yannick. It was a bit of a gamble because all the photographs had already been made. When we met in a café and I spread my images out in front of him, he immediately said to me: “I want to write a story about your photographs.” I wanted a fictional, novelistic text. He had carte blanche and made the work his own, while keeping certain fragments that were important to me, such as Tunisia, which is the country my parents come from. It gave me a way of going there, following in the footsteps of a youth I knew nothing about, as well as the extraordinary garden that once belonged to Leila Menchari. Eight months later, I received his text, which I obviously found very moving.

Is the woman you photograph, in some way, a self-portrait?

Carole Bellaïche: No, not at all. I have always photographed women who are the opposite of me. I have always had this fantasy of the blonde woman with light eyes. My mother was a redhead with green eyes, so perhaps that had some influence, it is possible… But I must also admit that what interests me more than self-portraiture is looking at the other.

You photograph faces extensively. What do you look for first in a gaze?

Carole Bellaïche: The most important thing for me is the intensity of the gaze. It is really what makes me want to photograph someone. There is something that passes through a gaze, something that can be very difficult to explain. I may be drawn to a face, but it is often the gaze that triggers the image. The artistic or aesthetic aspect, if you prefer, comes afterwards, with a certain harmony that allows me to explore its beauty. But beauty alone does not really interest me. What interests me is what lies behind it, what the face allows you to see. I like it when a photograph makes you want to keep looking, because you feel that there is something you cannot completely understand.

Do your images speak more of a presence, or of the possibility of an absence?

Carole Bellaïche: Instinctively, I would say: a presence. Even in the absence of certain places, there are traces of a presence. A photograph can show someone who is no longer there, but for me, what remains in the image is precisely that presence. A light, an object, a place, an attitude can be enough to make someone felt. I am not necessarily trying to photograph absence, but rather what remains of it, what continues to live in our memory. Perhaps that is also why certain images take on a different meaning over time. They become traces of something we have experienced, or something we have loved.

At what point does a photograph cease to be a memory and become fiction?

Carole Bellaïche: I think photography is always, to some extent, fiction. Even when it is very realistic, there is inevitably a choice, a framing, a light, a way of looking. For me, staging does not take anything away from the truth of an image. On the contrary, it can sometimes reveal something more intimate, something deeper. In this book, the characters really exist, their story really exists, but the images also tell something that may never actually have happened. That is where fiction becomes interesting.

After so many portraits, what remains elusive in a face?

Carole Bellaïche: Everything that cannot be seen. You can photograph a face, a gaze, an expression, but you never really know what is going on behind it. That is precisely what interests me. I can have the feeling that I know someone through a photograph and, at the same time, know that something is still escaping me. That is probably why I continue to photograph other people: to try to understand, even though I know I will never have the complete answer.

An exhibition is, I believe, set to follow the publication of the book. Could you tell us a little about it?

Carole Bellaïche: With pleasure. It will be a short exhibition. It opens on November 19th at Signature, Rue Jean-Pierre Thimbaud, with around forty black-and-white gelatin silver prints. There will be mainly still lifes.

Text and Interview by Carole Schmitz

title_original: A Low Hum: The 16th Gwangju Biennale
editorial_title_zh: 微弱低鸣：第16届光州双年展
editorial_excerpt_zh: 本届双年展将变革视为一种跨越不同尺度与节奏、层层交织的进程，它有时如地震般剧烈，有时又慢得难以察觉。路易斯·卢（Louis Lu）

article_text:
Shows

A Low Hum: The 16th Gwangju Biennale

JAMES T. HONG ’s

Apologies , 2012– , at “You must change your life,” the 16th Gwangju Biennale, 2026. Photo by Jeon Byung Cheol. Courtesy the Gwangju Biennale Foundation.

Each evening, the façade of the Gwangju Biennale Exhibition Hall lights up with James T. Hong’s Apologies (2012– ), an ever-expanding anthology of government officials and heads of state offering contrition. It is, in Hong’s words, “a timeline of political progress as unrepentant recidivism and contrite repetition.” The reel begins in 1937 with Japanese ambassador Hiroshi Saito regretting the sinking of the USS Panay, followed by German chancellor Willy Brandt falling to his knees before the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising monument, and closes in 2023 with the Dutch king apologizing for his nation’s role in slavery. In between, we see a procession of presidents, prime ministers, and a pope begging pardon for inherited legacies of discrimination, dispossession, and crimes. Delivered years, decades, sometimes centuries after the fact, these gestures accumulate into a tedious spectacle. What Hong’s work exposes, ultimately, is a paradox at the heart of any political change: the token of penitence stages transformation precisely in order to defer it. This monumental record of inertia is one of the few works in this year’s Gwangju Biennale that interrogates its title directive, “You Must Change Your Life,” showing how fast the imperative to transform can settle into ritual.

The directive itself is lifted from the closing line in Rainer Maria Rilke’s 1908 sonnet “Archaic Torso of Apollo.” Artistic director Ho Tzu Nyen has spoken of encountering the poem on an exhausted day and feeling an “expanded capacity.” The line carries urgency: it insists you change without explaining how or toward what. That openness allows Ho and his co-curators (Gahee Park, Brian Kuan Wood, and Che Kyongfa) to treat transformation as something layered across scales and rhythms, at times seismic, at times imperceptibly slow.

That split tempo is made tangible in the opening section, “Molecules and Me,” where Goldin+Senneby’s Resin Pond (2026) pools nearly two tons of pine resin across the floor into a luminous amber slick. Within the living tree, resin is at once a toxin that repels pests and fungi, and a sealant that closes wounds. It is also energy-dense, terpene-rich, harvestable for refinement into biodiesel and aviation fuel. Jakob Senneby, one half of the duo, lives with multiple sclerosis, a condition in which the body’s defenses chronically turn against its own nervous system. This experience with autoimmunity has reoriented the duo’s longstanding scrutiny of capital’s absurdities. Resin Pond proposes that the generative and the destructive are no longer separable—not in climate crisis, not in geopolitics, not in technology, and certainly not in the poison-cure logic of a market that carries within it both its own overcoming and its catastrophe: a perspective that regards change less as directional than conditional.

In the curatorial statement, Ho frames practices as techniques “repeated at regular intervals either to control or to conduct change,” and the tension between repetition and rupture runs through the exhibition. Scattered across the floors are clusters of volcanic rocks from Jeju, their contorted forms holding, within a single mass, radically unequal durations: the slow accrual of sediment, the violence of eruption, the long aftermath of cooling and weathering. Equally threaded through the space, and functioning as the exhibition’s connective tissue, are Sasaki Ken’s more than 60 small paintings of unremarkable things—a pair of Converse sneakers, workers’ boots, a light switch, a tennis ball. One of the canvases depicts an ominously overcast sky: Sasaki’s record of the Tokyo sky in the days after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake, when fears of radioactive drift from Fukushima hung in the air. Dispersed as they are, the rocks and the mundane paintings can feel opaque, even excessive. Yet their sheer persistence makes the argument that change moves at no single speed and takes no single form, and that it is often already underway, lodged in the textures of the everyday. Whether this constitutes a veiled hope for transformative force, or an oblique salute to Gwangju’s own insurgent heritage, the exhibition leaves deliberately open.

MAYA WATANABE ,

Liminal , 2019, still from video: 64 min. Produced by the Han Nefkens Foundation. Courtesy the artist.

“Molecules and Me” rewards sustained looking, and it repeatedly nudges the viewer toward the unfinished. Maya Watanabe’s Liminal (2019), a single-channel projection on a tilted, engulfing screen, offers extreme close-ups of human remains exhumed from mass graves of Peru’s internal armed conflict, which took place between 1980 and 2000. Decades later, roughly tens of thousands of the victims are still missing or nameless, and many crimes remain unacknowledged. Watanabe’s camera shifts constantly between focus and blur, refusing to let atrocity resolve into a fixed historical image. Even death, the work implies, withholds closure: mourning persists, identity stays suspended, and the past exerts its pressure from within a near-molecular anonymity.

Historical wounds and their seepage into daily life come to a point in the second section, “Bodies and Bonds,” where Mona Benyamin’s two videos furnish the exhibition’s most bracing case for art as a means of processing trauma. Her parents, who lived through the mass displacements of Palestinians during the Arab-Israeli conflicts, the Nakba (1948) and the Naksa (1967), are featured as performers cast into the formats of a sitcom and a newscast. In Trouble in Paradise (2018), they run through comic bits about the eradication of Palestinians, broaching the subject through gallows humor delivered with a Brechtian affect over a canned laugh track (“How do you make a Palestinian cry? You kill his family”). In Tomorrow, Again (2023), they reappear as anchors and bystanders: a newsreader who cannot stop weeping, an eyewitness to one disaster after another. Benyamin creates a condition of perpetual emergency and then asks, with a sardonic edge, how one is meant to change a life whose ground state is recurring ruin.

MONA BENYAMIN ,

Tomorrow, again , 2023, still from video, color, stereo sound: 11 min. Courtesy the artist.

SOHRAB HURA ,

Bittersweet , 2019, still from video: 13 min 48 sec. Courtesy the artist and Experimenter, Kolkata.

Time, kinship, and the slow labor of change take a more sensorial, elegiac turn in the pairing of Amanda Heng and Sohrab Hura. Heng’s Another Woman in Gwangju 1996, 2014, 2023 (2026) follows photographs of the artist and her mother across three decades, beginning with the mother’s request for a portrait and returning, in 2014 and again in 2023, to restage the original poses. As the two women age together, the roles of care and dependence visibly reverse, and the duration itself becomes legible. Nearby, Hura’s slideshow video Bittersweet (2019) and the black-and-white photographs, handwritten notes, and sketches of Life Is Elsewhere (2005–11) chronicle his life alongside a mother diagnosed with schizophrenia and her dog, Elsa. A letter penned by his mother details how the dog’s arrival remade her days: “As the years passed, I forgot all the reasons for not wanting her. She had become my dog and my friend a long time ago.” Change seldom arrives as a singular event, and neither do joy, grief, or hardship. It takes shape instead through fragments, the pieces by which a life is assembled.

From bodies and their bonds the exhibition widens to terrain and cosmos. Three works anchor “Cosmos and Change,” a darkened room of incantation and other-than-human vision: Bhenji Ra’s Biraddali Dancing on the Horizon (2024), drawn from the artist’s encounter with pangalay , a dance practiced by the Tausug of the Sulu Archipelago; Hura’s The Coast (2019), following devotees of the goddess Kali reveling in the roar of the surf on Tamil Nadu’s shores; and Saodat Ismailova’s enigmatic Melted into the Sun (2024), which trails an eighth-century mystic figure known as “The Veiled One” across the Amu Darya, the Chillpiq burial ground, and a Soviet-era solar furnace. The three soundtracks bleed into one another, wrapping the viewer in a field of moving images that is by turns harmonic and dissonant, and within which personal, familial, devotional, and national histories reveal themselves as continually rewritten by myth, ideology, and science.

JACQUELINE KIYOMI GORK ’s Not Exactly BPM (Variation Rrose), 2026. Commissioned by the 16th Gwangju Biennale, Supported by National Center for Art Research, Japan (NCAR), Tanoto Art Foundation (TAF), and Empty Gallery, Speaker equipment provided by Meyer Sound, Berkeley, CA. Courtesy Gwangju Biennale Foundation.

Jacqueline Kiyomi Gork’s Not Exactly BPM (Variation Rrose) (2026), presented in the final section, returns the focus to the body. It is a deconstructed nightclub built from centrifugal blowers, feedback, and transparent, sound-absorbing inflatables that swell into a sensory enclosure and then slowly exhale. A hypnotic score of kick drums and phase-shifting loops, built with the psychoacoustic artist Rrose, moves the room and its occupants alike. But instead of the euphoria of the dancefloor, the installation’s eerie self-awareness yields a low hum of anxiety and suspended anticipation, an artificial burnt-orange light filtering through vinyl walls.

Gork confronts the conceptually dense, politically freighted, and emotionally taxing works in the exhibition with a visceral reset, displacing intellectual reflection into corporeal attention: breath, pulse, the instability and the pleasure of an enclosed and rhythmic collective. If the biennale has spent its length imagining a “life elsewhere,” this last environment stages the pause before departure. It leaves the beholder with the question—how, having seen and felt all this, does one return to the world changed?

Louis Lu is an associate editor at ArtAsiaPacific.

article_text:
I t’s not quite up there with Leonardo DiCaprio eating raw bison liver to get into character, but Michelle Yeoh reportedly spent two years learning the Rubik’s Cube to prepare for this Chinese drama in which she plays a real-life former maths teacher who became a champion in retirement. The true story is stretched and squeezed here, fictionalised to fit sports-movie formula; it ends up being so-so entertaining and funny in places, but disappointingly predictable. The biggest surprise is that cubing is so popular it has its own world championship.

Still, Yeoh gives a superb, spiky performance as blunt, foul-tempered Zhao Yanhong; following a stroke, Zhao is living in a nursing home where she is the resident badass, assaulting her robot care companion and making illicit trips to the off-licence. She discovers her natural talent for the Rubik’s Cube when a washed-up ex-champion called Wu Youwei (Haoran Liu) comes to the nursing home to give a tutorial. What follows is a classic sports-film structure, with qualifying heats and Zhao training day and night, lifting weights and pounding the city streets. (Yes, running is de rigueur in a Rubik’s Cube movie; physical strength is Zhao’s weak spot says Wu, who agrees to be her coach.)

Yeoh is enjoyably irascible as Zhao, who goes viral after thrashing a kid in her first competition. Her online fans call her “Grandma Zhao” and the film gently chips away at stereotypes of the older generation; fans assume Zhao is a cuddly elder, while younger cubers underestimate her skill and stamina. Yeoh brings intelligence to the role, but it’s odd that after making Zhao so testy and short-tempered, the film is all soft edges with a squishy centre. Next, can we expect a biopic of the six-year-old Chinese girl who recently set a Rubik’s Cube world record , solving it in just over four seconds?

article_text:
T his weekend, the identity of the next James Bond is finally expected to be known – to the insiders, at least. According to reports, a number of youngish British actors – definitely three, possibly five – will have their final screen tests.

To say it has been a long time coming is an understatement. It is five years since Daniel Craig was killed in a hail of missiles at the end of No Time to Die, and in that time – even long before it – a swarm of actors have been tipped to replace him, only to age out of the role due to a combination of indecisiveness and cutthroat backstage corporate shenanigans. Whoever is declared to be 007 will be joining the franchise after what is likely to be the longest fallow period in the franchise’s 64-year history.

As such, this is kind of a big weekend. Let’s run through what we know so far.

The candidates

If three actors are to screen test for Bond this weekend, then they are Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Jack Lowden. If there are more – some outlets state that one other actor might be participating, others two – then they won’t include Jack O’Connell or Jacob Elordi , who are both out of the race for one reason or another.

The identity of the other actors are not yet known. Let’s take an uneducated guess and assume that one of them is a Beatle (the best fit is Harris Dickinson) and another one is more famous but less suitable (like Tom Cruise).

The screen test

Outlets are reporting that the screen test will encompass three main elements: stunts, camera presence and dialogue. These are all equally important for a modern Bond. Remove stunts from the equation and your film will be boring. Remove camera presence and you’re likely to end up with a George Lazenby type, who has the potential to fluff what would otherwise be an all-timer. Remove dialogue and you’re left with Quantum of Solace, and God knows we don’t need another one of those.

The chances

You could argue that Jack Lowden is the frontrunner, if only because the first scene of the first episode of Slow Horses was a pretty good Bond audition in itself. It was, you’ll remember, a race against time sprint through an airport and train station, on foot and in a car, complete with hand-to-hand combat and gun play. And it was very good indeed. Working against him is the sense that he’s a bit too much of a teddy bear for a sociopath like Bond. Plus the fact that he has spent every subsequent scene of Slow Horses doing a pretty good Simon Pegg impression.

Callum Turner would seem to make a sexier Bond, partly because he was able to conjure chemistry from the very silly sex purge movie One Night Only , and partly because he’s married to Dua Lipa, who would almost certainly get the role of Bond Girl Who Dies First if he were cast.

I still think Josh O’Connor would be the best fit, though. He looks good in a tux, as anyone who has seen The Crown will testify. He is very good at convincingly delivering absolute nonsense, as anyone who has seen Disclosure Day will testify. However, his best-known stunt work must be the long scene in The Mastermind in which he slowly climbs up and down a ladder several times in a row.

What’s missing?

Now, this is all well and good for a traditional Bond film. But we’re talking about an Amazon Bond film, directed by Denis Villeneuve . This means that more will be asked of whoever gets the role, and the screen tests are the perfect way to see if they can pull it off.

For example, which of the finalists will best be able to carry their voice in such a way that it isn’t drowned out by all the seat-rumbling full-volume honking noises that Villeneuve will almost certainly use instead of a traditional soundtrack? Which of the actors will most convincingly be able to interact with a side character created with the express purpose of carrying their own spin-off series, to better sustain cross-media IP synergy? Which of them will least overtly die on the inside during the scene in which an Amazon drone delivers them a gun? That is the stuff that will really make or break James Bond going forward.
